title: Metastable magnetic domains and the anomalous $B_\parallel=0$ resistance peak in twisted double bilayer graphene
authors: Zhenxiang Gao, Christopher Coleman, Silvia Folk, Ruiheng Su, Manabendra Kuiri, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Nemin Wei, Chunli Huang, Joshua Folk
abstract: In graphene moirés, valley polarization gives rise to orbital magnetism, manifested as an anomalous Hall effect and resulting in Barkhausen jumps in longitudinal resistance when changing domain configurations modify quasiparticle scattering. Beyond a simple picture of polarized domains, however, spin and valley textures within and between the domains are less well understood, as is the effect of these textures on transport. In the valley-polarized quarter-metal state of twisted double bilayer graphene, a sharp and metastable peak in longitudinal resistance often appears at zero in-plane magnetic field, whose microscopic origin has yet to be identified. Here, we show that this peak depends on the configuration of domains of orbital magnetism, which is itself set by the gate-voltage trajectory used to enter the ordered state and by the magnetic field --- particularly the in-plane component --- present during that trajectory. The sensitivity of the effect to in-plane magnetic field components points to spin, linked to valley polarization through spin-orbit coupling, as the key degree of freedom in both the domain formation and the resistance peak.
summary: This work investigates an anomalous resistance peak at zero in-plane magnetic field in twisted double bilayer graphene. The authors show this peak is highly sensitive to how the material reaches its electronic state, pointing to a mechanism rooted in the domain structure of orbital magnetism. They argue that spin, coupled to valley polarization via spin-orbit interaction, is the key degree of freedom governing this exotic transport signature.
main_problem: The paper investigates the microscopic origin of a sharp, metastable peak in longitudinal resistance ($R_{xx}$) observed precisely at zero in-plane magnetic field ($B_\parallel=0$) in twisted double bilayer graphene.
main_result: The peak's existence and magnitude are highly sensitive to the history of gate-voltage sweeps and the applied magnetic field, strongly suggesting it is governed by the domain structure of orbital magnetism, which involves spin textures.
method: The study uses low-temperature transport measurements, mapping $R_{xx}$ and $R_{xy}$ as functions of gate voltages and applied in-plane magnetic fields, complemented by differential resistance measurements.
model_or_system: The physical system is twisted double bilayer graphene (t2+2) operating in a valley-polarized quarter-metal state. The physics involves moiré superlattices, orbital magnetism, and the interplay between valley, spin, and charge degrees of freedom.
key_observables: Longitudinal resistance $R_{xx}(B_\parallel)$, anomalous Hall resistance $R_{xy}$, and differential resistance $	ext{dV}_{xx}/	ext{dI}$ vs. bias current $	ext{I}_{	ext{DC}}$.
important_parameters: Low temperatures (100-300 mK), in-plane magnetic field components ($B_x, B_y$), and the gate-voltage trajectory used to prepare the electronic state.
main_assumptions: The peak is attributed to metastable magnetic domain configurations, and the underlying physics involves spin-transfer torques acting on domain walls.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate $R_{xx}(B_\parallel)$ scans showing the $B_\parallel=0$ peak, demonstrating its dependence on the approach path (gate voltage trajectory) and its robustness against out-of-plane fields ($B_z$).
paper_structure: The paper systematically maps the resistance landscape by varying gate voltages and magnetic fields, establishing the dependence of the $B_\parallel=0$ peak on the preparation history, and finally proposing a mechanism involving spin-transfer torques at domain walls.
why_interesting: The strong coupling between transport measurements and the history-dependent formation of magnetic domains touches upon non-equilibrium dynamics and emergent topological phenomena, which are relevant to understanding quantum state preparation in condensed matter systems.
